title: Chapter 7 – Iron and Wine
html:
Old Hu arrives eight days later on a mule cart, and the whole of Green Pine Hill comes out to watch.

The cart creaks up the gate road piled so high with iron that the mule leans into its collar like a man pushing a wall. A small anvil sits lashed in the center like a squat black idol. Behind it, the folded leather lungs of a pair of bellows, and six wine jars packed in straw. Old Hu walks beside the mule with the reins in his one hand and does not look up at the crowd at all.

Fourth Uncle's guards at the gate stare at the empty sleeve. The servants in the courtyard stare at the jars. On the steps of the main hall, half the family has gathered with the expressions of people who have heard rumors and want to see whether they are true.

Lin Hu, nine years old and at the second layer and anxious to be noticed, walks over to the cart as it comes to a stop, looks the one-armed refiner up and down, and spits on the wheel.

There is a short, sharp silence.

Old Hu looks at the spittle on his wheel. Then he looks at the boy. He does not say anything. He does not need to. Lin Hu takes a step backward, then another, and then his mother has him by the ear and is dragging him away and apologizing to nobody in particular in a high, rapid voice.

Old Hu turns back to the cart and begins to untie the anvil.

\ \ \*

Grandfather receives him in the main hall, with the family in their places along the walls.

Lin Zhenshan sits in the Patriarch's chair in his good robe, his white beard combed. Old Hu stands before him in a clean leather apron that still smells of the forge. Neither of them speaks for a long moment.

Then Lin Jian feels it.

Two pressures, rising: his grandfather's, vast and steady as water filling a basin, and Old Hu's, dense and hot as the air before a furnace. Ninth layer meeting ninth layer. Neither man moves. But on the table between them, the tea in the cups has begun to tremble.

It lasts perhaps three breaths. Then both pressures sink back, as if by agreement, and the tea goes still.

Old Hu bows. Exactly as deeply as courtesy requires, not a hair further. Lin Jian has seen that bow before, from Zhao Heng, and he sees Grandfather notice it, and he sees something in the old man's face that might be amusement.

"Guest Elder Hu," says Lin Zhenshan. "My daughter-in-law tells me you are a refiner."

"I was," says Old Hu. "Now I fix hoes."

"She tells me you are going to teach my grandson."

"If he wants teaching."

"And what will you teach him? The forge? Weapons?" Grandfather's eyes are sharp. "He has a five-element root, Guest Elder. You know what that means."

"I don't teach roots," says Old Hu. "Never have. I teach hands." He holds up his one scarred hand. "And eyes."

For a moment, Grandfather says nothing at all. Then something happens to his face that Lin Jian has not seen in a long time. It crinkles. Around the eyes first, then in the deep lines at the corners of his mouth, and then the old man throws back his head and laughs, a big, rusty, startled laugh that fills the whole hall and goes on for some time.

Everyone stares at him. Lin Jian has never once heard his grandfather laugh in front of the family.

"Hands and eyes," the Patriarch says, wiping his own eyes. "Hands and eyes. Very well, Hu Tieshou. Teach him hands and eyes."

\ \ \*

The terms are settled that afternoon, and Second Uncle argues against every one of them.

Old Hu will have a room in the eastern wing, and the old granary by the east wall for his forge, which has stood empty since the last bad harvest. He will mend the family's tools and the village's, for nothing. He will take his meals with the household. He will have a jar of wine a week.

"Whose wine?" says Second Uncle pleasantly. "The household's wine allowance is already stretched, Father. And a guest elder of the ninth layer usually draws a stipend. Twenty stones a year at the least. With the tribute as it is—"

"From my own allowance," says Grandfather.

"Father—"

"The wine comes from my own allowance, Wenhai."

"And the stipend?"

"Don't want it," says Old Hu, from the end of the table. Every head turns. "I'm not cultivating. What would I do with stones?" He drinks his tea. "Give me charcoal and iron and the boy, and leave me alone."

Second Uncle smiles and nods and writes something in his book. Lin Jian, watching from behind his father's shoulder, sees the hand that holds the silver pencil go very still for a moment, and then move on.

The last term is the only one Old Hu insists on.

"The boy's my apprentice," he says. "Only him. Nobody else's children in my forge. Nobody tells me how to teach him. Nobody asks him what I teach him." He looks around the table. "Those are my terms."

Grandfather looks at him a long time.

"Agreed," he says.

\ \ \*

They build the forge in five days.

The old granary is a stone building with a slate roof, a beaten-earth floor, and a single wide door facing the courtyard. It smells of mice and old rice. Old Hu walks around it once, slowly, tapping the walls with his knuckles, kicking at the floor, looking up at the roof beams, and then says, "Here," and points at the northeast corner, where the floor is solid flagstone over bedrock.

Then he makes Lin Jian carry bricks.

Fire bricks, from the family's old kiln on the lowest terrace, four at a time and then three and then two, in a basket on his back. Old Hu lays them one-handed, buttering each with clay and tapping it home with the heel of a trowel, never once going back to adjust one. A hearth takes shape in the corner, waist high, with a deep firepot and a hood to catch the smoke. The bellows go in beside it. A channel is cut through the wall for the blast pipe. The anvil, which weighs as much as a grown man, Old Hu moves himself, rocking it end over end across the floor with his one arm and his knee, grunting, while Lin Jian holds his breath.

It is during those five days that Lin Jian scans the rest of the old refiner's life.

The anvil, on the second day, while Hu is fetching water.

```
[Scan: Anvil]
Body: cast iron
Face: forge-welded plate of spirit steel (Yellow grade), Qi-hardened by long use
Note: Absorbed Qi residue from ~40 years of Qi-assisted forging
Creation Energy +8 (67 / 100)
```

A long iron rod, as thick as Lin Jian's wrist and as tall as he is, which leans in the corner by the door and which Old Hu, he notices, never lets out of arm's reach.

```
[Scan: Iron Rod]
Material: spirit iron (Yellow grade, high), folded 64 times
Note: weapon-grade construction disguised as a pry bar
Creation Energy +5 (72 / 100)
```

The tongs, the bellows' leather, a pot of black flux, a point or two each.

```
Creation Energy: 81 / 100
```

And on the fifth day, when the hearth is finished and Old Hu lights the first fire in it, a small hammer.

It is the smallest of the hammers that hang over the new forge, with a head no bigger than an egg and a handle of pale hickory worn so smooth that it looks like old ivory. Old Hu hangs it in the place of honor, at the center of the rack, and touches it once with his fingertips before he turns away. Later, while he is out in the courtyard arguing with Fourth Uncle about charcoal, Lin Jian stands on a crate and lays one finger on the hammer's head.

```
[Scan: Refiner's Hammer (Small)]
Head: tool steel, hand-forged; maker's mark on cheek: hammer over wave
Handle: hickory, approx. 50 years of use
Note: Exceptional craftsmanship. Maker's Qi residue: present, old.
Creation Energy +6 (87 / 100)
```

A mark on the cheek of the hammerhead, so worn he can barely see it with his eyes: a small hammer above three curved lines, like waves.

He gets down off the crate just before Old Hu comes back in.

\ \ \*

Lin Feng does not like it.

He does not say so. He rises before dawn now and goes down to the gate yard with his spear, and Lin Jian goes with him, as promised, and shows him the fire ring: not big, but fast and low and placed, a hoop of flame that springs up under an opponent's feet. On the fifth morning Lin Feng brings it up under Old Gou, who has come down early to watch, and the farmer leaps a foot in the air and lands on his backside, and Lin Feng laughs so hard he has to sit down.

But in the afternoons, when Lin Jian goes into the granary and Old Hu closes the door, Lin Feng stands in the courtyard and looks at the closed door for a long time before he walks away. "I asked the refiner to teach me spear work," he says at dinner, to no one. "He said he makes spears, he doesn't teach them."

"Then learn it from your Fourth Uncle," says Grandfather. "He's better than any refiner."

\ \ \*

On the evening of the fifth day, when the fire has burned down to coals and the forge is quiet, Old Hu sits on the anvil block with a jar of wine and looks at Lin Jian across the dark granary.

"When we shook hands," he says. "In my ravine."

Lin Jian, who has been sweeping the floor, stops.

"I felt something," says Old Hu. "Cold. Like a thread of water. It went in through my palm and up my arm and into my shoulder, and it looked around in there, and then it went away." He takes a drink. "That was you."

It is not a question, so Lin Jian does not answer it. He thinks very fast.

If you ever lie to me, boy, I'll know.

"I felt something too," he says carefully. Every word true. "In your shoulder. Something cold. It didn't belong to you. It was eating you." He hesitates. "I'm sorry. I didn't mean to look."

The forge is very quiet. A coal settles in the hearth.

"Eating me," Old Hu repeats.

"Yes."

"Something that didn't belong to me."

"Yes."

Old Hu sets the jar down very carefully on the floor beside the anvil. He sits for a long moment with his hand on his knee, staring at nothing. When he speaks again his voice is quite different, low and rough.

"Three healers," he says. "A Nascent Soul elder. A Nascent Soul elder, boy, who could have counted the hairs on my head from across a room. He went through my shoulder with his spiritual sense like a comb through wool, and he found nothing. My own Qi, he said. A furnace sickness." He looks at Lin Jian. "And a seven-year-old five-element root shakes my hand and finds it in a heartbeat."

Lin Jian says nothing.

"Spiritual sense," Old Hu says slowly, half to himself. "That's what it must be. Some children are born with it stronger than their roots. But not like this. Never like this." He looks up sharply. "Does anyone else know?"

"My mother knows I feel things."

"Your mother knows a lot of things she doesn't say." Old Hu leans forward. "Listen to me. You tell no one what you felt in my shoulder. You tell no one you can feel things in people's channels at all. If the wrong person learns that a boy on this hill can see what a Nascent Soul elder can't, you won't live to be ten." He sits back. "Understand?"

"Yes."

"Good." He picks up the jar again, and drinks, and for a while neither of them says anything. Then, very quietly, to the fire: "Blood Qi. I knew it. I knew it the night it happened. Fifteen years everyone telling me I was imagining it." He laughs, without any humor. "Well. Now I know I'm not mad. That's something."

Lin Jian sweeps the last of the floor and does not ask what happened fifteen years ago.

\ \ \*

His body training begins the next morning.

"Your Qi is a trickle," says Old Hu, standing over him in the gray dawn by the river at the foot of the hill. "Five elements fighting over a ditch. You'll fill your dantian eventually. Slowly. Your grandfather thinks it will take you thirty years to reach the fifth layer, and he might be right." He kicks a basket across the gravel toward him. "But the body doesn't care about roots. The body is a body. Iron is iron. You temper it the same way whatever it came out of."

He explains it, in his rough, short sentences, while Lin Jian stares at the basket.

The old body cultivators, the ones who forged their flesh instead of their Qi, say there are nine realms of the body, just as there are nine great realms of Qi. Most never pass the first. Skin Tempering, when the skin learns to hold Qi like a soaked hide holds water and a common blade slides off it. Then Flesh Forging, when the muscles thicken and toughen and a man can lift an ox. Then Bone Forging, when the bones themselves grow dense as iron. "And past that," Old Hu says, "Blood Refining, and things I've only read about in books I couldn't afford. Don't worry about those. Worry about your skin."

"How?"

Old Hu points at the river gravel, and the basket, and the hill.

Lin Jian carries eleven baskets up the hill to the granary that first morning. By the last one his legs are shaking so hard that he falls on the steps and spills half of it. Old Hu watches him pick up every stone, one at a time, and says nothing.

Then there is the bath.

Old Hu brews it in an iron pot on the new forge, in a cloud of evil-smelling steam: iron-root vine, which burns; red-pepper bark, which burns worse; and a gray powder of burnt bone, which makes the whole mixture thick and gritty. He pours it into a wooden tub, lets it cool until it is merely painful, and tells Lin Jian to get in and stay in for an hour.

It feels as if his skin is being peeled off by a thousand small, hot fingers. He clenches his teeth and runs the Five-Gate Wheel, because it gives his mind something to do other than scream.

"Rogue method," says Old Hu, sitting on a crate beside the tub with his jar. "No sect would teach it. Too slow, too painful, and it doesn't make anybody rich. My master taught it to me when I was your age, because he said a refiner who couldn't take a burn should go and be a farmer." He drinks. "Skin first, then flesh, then bone. Every day. No days off."

"For how long?" Lin Jian manages.

"For as long as it takes. Took me three years to reach Skin Tempering." He considers. "A five-element root, with no Qi to speak of to push it along? Five. Maybe six."

When the hour is up, Lin Jian climbs out of the tub, red from head to foot, and stands dripping on the flagstones, and notices something.

His skin prickles. Not with pain. With something else, faint and new: a sense of fullness under the surface, as if the skin itself has been soaked in Qi and is reluctant to let it go.

While Old Hu is emptying the tub, he dips a finger in the dregs of the bath.

```
[Scan: Body Tempering Decoction (Crude)]
Iron-root sap: 18% extracted
Red-pepper bark: 34% extracted
Bone ash: largely undissolved (particle size too coarse)
Effectiveness: Low
Blueprint: Saved
Note: Optimization possible.
Creation Energy +1 (88 / 100)
```

Eighteen percent. Thirty-four. Undissolved.

He looks at the gritty gray sludge in the bottom of the tub and begins, very quietly, to smile.

In the weeks that follow, Old Hu also teaches him the Ironhide Art, a Mortal-rank method of driving Qi into the skin in the moment before a blow lands. It needs no root, only enough Qi to push and a body that has learned to hold it. By the end of the first month Lin Jian can tense his forearm and take a smack from Old Hu's practice stick without crying out. By the end of the second, he can take it without flinching.

"Better," says Old Hu, which from him is a speech.

\ \ \*

His days take on a shape.

Before dawn, the wheel, with his mother by the door. At first light, the gate yard with Lin Feng, then the river and the gravel baskets. Mornings in the courtyard with Uncle Mao. Afternoons in the granary. And in the hour before dinner, when the others are washing or resting, he goes up onto the empty threshing floor behind the storehouse and practices, alone, the way he once practiced lab procedures: the same motion, slowly, a hundred times, until his hands do it without him.

The Five-Element Ward Art, on scrapes and blisters and the burns Old Hu's forge gives him every day. Forty percent now. Earthen Rampart, a shin-high ridge, then a knee-high one, then a shin-high one raised in half a breath. And his third art, the one Uncle Mao begins teaching the children that autumn: Cloudstep.

It is a wind art, a Mortal-rank vortex that spins up out of a twist of the wrists and knocks an enemy's feet out from under him. The children practice it on leaves. Lin Jian practices it on leaves too, at first. His vortex is a sad thing, a little eddy that stirs the pine needles and dies. Wind is not one of the five elements. It belongs, Uncle Mao says, to wood and metal together, the breath of the forest and the edge of the blade, and a cultivator who can only feed his elements one at a time should not be able to cast it at all.

So he stops trying to feed them together. He feeds wood through the first half of the twist and metal through the second, like two gears meshing, and on the ninth evening the needles on the threshing floor rise up in a hissing spiral as tall as he is and scatter across the roof of the storehouse.

He stands in the middle of the swept circle with his hands still twisted and his heart pounding, and looks up, and sees his father on the storehouse steps.

Lin Wenyuan has a scroll case under his arm and an odd expression on his face. He looks at the swept circle, and at his son, and at the pine needles still drifting down off the roof.

"Uncle Mao says you've been practicing up here every evening," he says.

"Yes, Father."

His father comes and sits down on the edge of the threshing floor with a grunt, the scroll case across his knees. For a while he says nothing. Then he opens the case.

Inside, on a bed of folded silk, lie three yellow talismans, each as long as Lin Jian's hand. He knows them all from the shop: a Fire Starter, a Lesser Flame-Burst, and a Mirror Guard. But these are not shop talismans. The characters on them are drawn with a care he has never seen in his father's work, every stroke clean and unbroken, every curl closed, as if the brush has been held by a steady hand.

"I made these for you," his father says. "One at a time. Over a month." He smiles a little. "It took me thirty tries for the Flame-Burst."

Lin Jian looks up at him.

"You're going into the mountains with your mother. You're spending your days in a forge with a man who drinks. And you're up here every evening teaching yourself wind arts that a five-element root should not be able to cast so well." His father closes the case and puts it in his hands. "I can't do much, Jian. My hand isn't what it was. But I can do this." He taps the case. "The Fire Starter you know. The Mirror Guard you tear across, so, and say guard, and it holds for five breaths. The Flame-Burst you throw, and say burst, and don't be standing near it. Never use the Flame-Burst unless you mean it. And never, ever use it indoors."

"Yes, Father."

"Keep them on you. Always." His father gets up, stiffly, and looks down at him. "And when you've used them, come and tell me, and I'll make you more."

He goes down the steps. Lin Jian sits on the threshing floor with the case in his lap and does not open it again for a long time.

\ \ \*

Old Hu's gift comes a week later, without ceremony.

Lin Jian comes into the granary one afternoon and finds a bracer lying on the workbench: a band of dark bronze as long as his forearm, cut down from one of Fourth Uncle's guard arm-guards, with a thin line of spirit copper hammered into a channel along its length and a new glyph etched on the inner face, smaller and finer than the one the Willow Ford refiner put there.

"Bled on it yet?" says Old Hu from the forge, without turning round.

"It's for me?"

"Your uncle broke the strap on that one and was going to throw it away. Shoddy work. Willow Ford refiner doesn't know how to lay a channel." He pumps the bellows. "I relaid the copper and cut the glyph again. It'll hold three breaths longer than it did, and it'll come back in four hours instead of six. Still Mortal grade. I'm not making you anything better until you've proved you won't lose it in a river."

Lin Jian picks it up. It is warm from the forge, and heavier than it looks.

```
[Scan: Mantle Bracer (Mortal Grade, High)]
Barrier duration: +60% over original
Recharge: ~4 hours (ambient Qi)
Craftsmanship: excellent
Creation Energy +0 (variant of known blueprint)
```

He pricks his thumb on the edge of the workbench, and presses the bead of blood to the glyph, and feels the bracer settle against his arm like a hand closing around his wrist.

"Thank you," he says.

Old Hu grunts. "Wear it in the tub," he says. "Iron-root sap eats spirit copper if you're not used to it. You might as well both learn."

It is, Lin Jian realizes later, the first thing Old Hu has made with his own hands since he came up the hill that is not a hoe.

\ \ \*

On the twenty-third night after the forge is finished, Lin Jian wakes in the dark to the sound of voices from the granary.

His room shares a wall with the eastern wing. Old Hu's room is on the other side of the courtyard, but in the stillness of the small hours, sound carries across the stones, and there is only one voice in the house that sounds like warm honey poured over something sharp.

He slips out of bed. His mother, who sleeps lightly, does not stir, or pretends not to.

He crouches in the shadow of the woodpile by the eastern wall with his back to the stones and listens.

"I'm only saying," Second Uncle is saying, "that a man of your skill is wasted here, Elder Hu. Wasted. Mending hoes for a family that can barely pay its tribute." The clink of a jar. "That is Cloud Mist Peach Wine, by the way. Very rare. I thought you might appreciate it."

Old Hu says nothing.

"There are families in this county," Second Uncle goes on, "with Foundation Establishment elders and second-grade veins and furnaces that would make you weep, who would pay a great deal for a refiner of the ninth layer. A very great deal. Forty stones a year, to start. More, once they saw your work." A pause. "All you would have to do, in the meantime, is stay here. Teach the boy. And now and then, let me know how things are. How my father's health is. Whether he is cultivating more, or less. Whether he coughs." Another pause, gentler. "Families like that like to plan ahead, you see. And an old man's health is such an uncertain thing."

There is a silence.

Then there is the sound of a chair scraping back, and a heavy tread on the stones, and the granary door banging open so hard that it bounces off the wall.

"Get out," says Old Hu.

"Elder Hu, I think you misunder—"

"I said get out. And take your peach wine with you, or I'll pour it down your neck."

Lin Jian, pressed against the woodpile, sees his uncle come out of the granary door into the moonlight. Wenhai's face is pale, and his smile is gone. He is holding a small blue jar against his chest. He looks back at the door once, and his eyes in the moonlight are like a cat's, flat and bright and thinking. Then he walks quickly away across the courtyard toward the main hall.

The granary door slams.

\ \ \*

In the morning, without looking up from the bellows, Old Hu says: "Your uncle came to see me last night."

"I know," says Lin Jian. "I heard."

Old Hu glances at him and grunts. He pumps the bellows. The coals flare orange.

"Forty stones a year," he says. "From families with Foundation elders." He spits into the fire. "That wasn't Lin money, boy."

"No," says Lin Jian. "It wasn't."

That afternoon, as he promised on the eastern wall, he goes to find his grandfather.

The old man is in the library, sitting in the dark with his pipe, as he so often is. He listens to the whole thing without moving: the peach wine, the forty stones, the families with Foundation elders, the questions about whether he coughs.

When Lin Jian has finished, his grandfather is silent for a long time.

"Forty stones a year," he says at last. "And the Lin treasury cannot spare twenty for a guest elder's stipend." He taps the pipe against his palm. "Your uncle has deep pockets, for a man who keeps such careful accounts."

"Yes, Grandfather."

The old man looks at him in the dim light from the door. "You did well to come to me. You will say nothing of this to anyone else. Not your father. Not Old Hu. Old Hu already knows, and your father," he pauses, "your father has enough to carry."

"Yes, Grandfather."

"Go back to your forge, little builder."

Lin Jian goes. At the door he looks back, and sees the old man still sitting in the dark with the cold pipe in his hand, looking at the bottom shelf where Second Uncle keeps his old account books.

\ \ \*

He finishes the last scan he needs that night, in the dark granary, after Old Hu has gone to bed.

It is not anything grand. It is the old refiner's leather case of fine tools, which Hu has finally opened that evening to show him how to cut a file, and left on the bench. Inside, wrapped in oiled cloth, are a dozen slender iron spikes etched along their length with lines so fine he can barely see them, and a handful of dark metal discs no bigger than coins.

He does not know what they are. He lays his hand on the cloth.

```
[Scan: Etched Iron Spikes (12) / Metal Discs (6)]
Function: unknown (insufficient data)
Structure: Qi-conductive etched channels; discs show charge-storage lattice
Note: Components of a larger system
Creation Energy +12 (100 / 100)
```

The panel freezes.

Then it goes white.

Not the soft blue of an ordinary scan. A hard, bright white that floods his whole vision, so sudden and so complete that he grabs the edge of the workbench to keep from falling. Through it, like letters surfacing in a photographic tray, words begin to form.

```
[Creation Energy Threshold Reached]
[Interface Upgrade in Progress]

ARK-7 Fabrication Interface — Level 1 → Level 2
Designation: REFINER

New capabilities:
— Fabrication: low-grade spirit materials (Yellow grade)
— Pill Synthesis: from scanned or observed recipes (Grade 1–2)
— Separation: extract components from non-living mixtures
— Formation Components: low-grade (requires scanned reference)
— Spirit Tools: low-grade

Locked: living tissue, Profound grade and above, spirit stones

Creation Energy: 0 / 400
```

The white fades. The blue returns. The granary is dark and cold and smells of coal, and nothing in it has changed.

Lin Jian stands by the workbench with his hand on a leather case of spikes he does not understand, breathing hard, and reads the panel again.

Pill Synthesis. Grade one to two.

He thinks about a bronze cauldron like a fat green toad, and a tired woman pushing her Qi into it until her hands shake, and a dark brown pill that is two-thirds charcoal.

He thinks about what a Breath-Gathering Pill would do to the Five-Gate Wheel if it were not thirty parts in a hundred good, but ninety-nine.

Then he wraps the spikes back in their cloth exactly as Old Hu left them, and closes the case, and goes to bed. He does not sleep.

Across the courtyard, in the eastern wing, a lamp is still burning in Old Hu's window, and it burns there until dawn.
